While I personally come down very hard on Hillary for this one, there's a big difference between knowingly and purposely disseminating a metric ton of privileged/classified information and potentially leaking a much smaller amount of it unintentionally due to ignorance or laziness. Neither are okay (though I would argue Snowden was right to do much of what he did), but we shouldn't be drawing a false equivalence either.

I'm pretty sure moving top secret files to a non-secure, unapproved location is a statutory crime, rather than a traditional mens rea crime. As such, it doesn't matter if it was actually utterly ineptitude on her part, or a malicious attempt to hide and delete politically embarassing emails.

The term you're looking for is probably "strict liability offense," which some people confuse with "statutory" due to the insanity with which some US states apply strict liability to (most commonly) statutory rape (which itself is a colloquial term used to describe cases which are criminalized by a statute prohibition rather than the lack of consent which characterized rape in common law). You're right, though, that what distinguishes a strict liability offense is the removal of the mens rea requirement - lack of intent is not a defense, though some jurisdictions do still allow "due diligence" defenses for such offenses and may have an even higher category where those aren't permitted. (Canada is the one that comes to mind for me: we have "strict" liability which allows a due diligence defense and "absolute" liability which does not.)

Regardless, no. I don't claim to be an expert on the relevant laws, but the primary issue for Clinton is probably a much simpler policy violation. Now, policy violations at that level can lead to all sorts of nasty stuff (and are usually treated as strict liability, since the employees involved are expected to know the policy), but they're not "crimes" in the sense we're talking about. The law that is usually relevant to classified information is the Espionage Act (18 USC ch. 37, 791-799), which has indeed been interpreted to be a mens rea offense. This isn't exactly surprising, since the relevant sections all contain text to the tune of "Whoever...having possession of...any document...or information relating to the national defense which information the possessor has reason to believe could be used to the injury of the United States....willfully communicates, delivers, transmits...to any person not entitled to receive it..." (Stupidly redacted, yes, but you'll understand why if you read the original.) The most relevant of these would be section 798, which applies to a relatively limited subset of classified information (specifically communication intelligence) and reads, "Whoever knowingly and willfully communicates, furnishes, transmits, or otherwise makes available to an unauthorized person, or publishes, or uses in any manner prejudicial to the safety or interest of the United States or for the benefit of any foreign government to the detriment of the United States any classified information [on this subsequent list]." In addition to the Espionage Act (which, as mentioned, covers only national defense information) there's also the Intelligence Identities Protection Act, which covers covert agents (whether or not the information is classified) and the Atomic Energy Act, but both have similar intent provisions.

As it stands, Hillary is probably guilty of a strict liability policy violation while being innocent of any crime related to classified information - ineptitude isn't an excuse for her not following policy, but it does mean that she deserves workplace sanctions rather than an orange jumpsuit (at least as far as her handling of classified material goes).
